introduction_markdown: CAMEROON GENERAL CERTIFICATE OF EDUCATION BOARD, General Certificate of Education Examination. 0785 Religious Studies 1, JUNE 2022, ADVANCED LEVEL. Multiple choice question paper, one and a half hours. Mobile phones are NOT allowed in the examination room. Instructions to candidates: use a soft HB pencil throughout the examination; do not open the booklet until told to do so; check that the booklet is headed 'Advanced Level - 0785 Religious Studies 1'; fill in the information required on the answer sheet (Candidate Name, Exam Session, Subject Code and Candidate Identification Number). Answer ALL the 50 questions in this Examination. All questions carry equal marks. Each question has FOUR suggested answers: A, B, C and D. Decide which answer is correct, find the number of the question on the answer sheet and draw a horizontal line across the letter to join the square brackets for the answer you have chosen. Mark only one answer for each question: if you mark more than one answer you will score a zero for that question. If you change your mind about an answer, erase the first mark carefully and then mark your new answer. Avoid spending too much time on any one question; you can come back to it later. Do all rough work in this booklet, using the blank spaces. At the end of the examination the invigilator collects the answer sheet first and then the question booklet.

Clés interprétatives à relire : 2 (Isaac, « Covenant Child »), 6 (Ishmaélites, alors que le texte biblique cite aussi des Madianites), 8 (Exodus plutôt que Passover), 12 (Salomon, David ayant préparé le Temple), 23 (Eightfold path plutôt que Four noble truths), 33 (Khadija ; la tradition cite aussi Ali et Abu Bakr comme premiers dans leurs catégories), 41 (Caliphs ; les chiites parlent d'Imams), 44, 47, 50 (généralités sur les religions africaines traditionnelles, qui varient selon les peuples).

Questions du sujet imprimé dont la clé n'est pas établie de façon sûre, converties en questions ouvertes : 11 (la tribu de Saul est Benjamin, absente des options : Kish est son père), 25 (le lotus symbolise la pureté et l'éveil, aucune option exacte), 27 (Vedas, Brahmanas et Upanishads défendables, « Ashanyankas » non identifiable), 30 (énoncé « spread through » vague), 45 (aucun fait classique pour désigner la malédiction), 47 (« major type of worship » discutable) et 48 (« essence of African morality » diffère selon les auteurs).

Coquilles du sujet imprimé recopiées telles quelles dans les options : « Cannanites » (Q6), « Epharath » (Q3), « Hadikkah » et « Hanukkah » pour deux options distinctes (Q20), « Samrara » (Q24), « Ashanyankas » (Q27), « Kharma » (Q30), « Mosksha » (Q29), « Daouda » (Q31, Q34), « Abu Bar » (Q33), « Wahabis » et « Tijannis » (Q43), « Here-After » (Q44). Les corrigés rétablissent la bonne graphie sans changer les options.

Q36 : le sujet parle de la part du « revenu » ; le zakat est en réalité calculé sur la richesse conservée un an au-delà du seuil (nisab), ce que le corrigé précise. La neutralité entre traditions est respectée (formulations « according to Islamic tradition », « Muslims believe »).

L'option D de la question 9 (« Jerusalem. ») est imprimée en haut de la colonne de droite de la page 2 (sous le groupe d'options de la question 9) ; elle est rattachée à la question 9. Aucune règle de choix : tout le paper est obligatoire (regles_choix vide).
Converties en questions ouvertes par le relecteur (clé ou options discutables) : 11, 25, 27, 30, 45, 47, 48.

questions.enonce_markdown: He is known in history as the father of the Hebrew nation:
questions.corrige_markdown: Abraham (Abram) is the ancestor of the Hebrew nation: in Genesis 12 and 15 God called him and promised him descendants who would become a great nation, and the Israelites trace their descent through his son Isaac and his grandson Jacob. Moses is the leader of the Exodus and the mediator of the Law, while Isaac and Jacob are Abraham's son and grandson. **Answer: D.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - patriarchs of israel

questions.enonce_markdown: He was the Covenant Child:
questions.corrige_markdown: Isaac was the child of the promise, born to Abraham and Sarah in their old age, and God said that his covenant would be continued through him (Genesis 17 and 21). Abraham received the covenant but was not the child of it, Jacob was a later heir and Moses belongs to the Exodus and the Sinai covenant. **Answer: C.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - patriarchs of israel

questions.enonce_markdown: Abraham buried his wife, Sarah, in a cave at:
questions.corrige_markdown: Genesis 23 tells how Abraham bought the cave of Machpelah, near Hebron, from Ephron the Hittite so that he could bury Sarah. Jericho is a city taken by Joshua, Qumran is the site linked with the Dead Sea Scrolls, and Ephrath (printed 'Epharath') is the place near which Rachel was buried (Genesis 35). **Answer: B.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - patriarchs of israel

questions.enonce_markdown: Who bore the nick - name of 'Supplanter'?
questions.corrige_markdown: The name Jacob is linked in Genesis with the idea of grasping the heel and supplanting: Jacob took Esau's birthright and then the blessing of the firstborn (Genesis 25 and 27), and Esau remarks that he has supplanted him twice. Esau was the one supplanted, and Isaac and Laban were not given this nickname. **Answer: A.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - patriarchs of israel

questions.enonce_markdown: Who was the brain behind Jacob's trick against the father?
questions.corrige_markdown: Rebekah (printed 'Rebecca') planned the deception in which Jacob, dressed in Esau's clothes and wearing goatskins, brought food to the blind Isaac to receive the blessing meant for Esau (Genesis 27). Leah and Rachel were Jacob's wives, and Zipporah was the wife of Moses. **Answer: C.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - patriarchs of israel

questions.enonce_markdown: The merchants who bought Joseph as a slave were called:
questions.corrige_markdown: In Genesis 37 Joseph's brothers sold him to a caravan of traders described as Ishmaelites (the same chapter also calls the traders Midianites, who are not among the options), and they took him to Egypt. The Egyptians only bought him later, in Egypt (Genesis 37 and 39), and the Philistines and Canaanites (printed 'Cannanites') are not the traders of this story. **Answer: B.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - patriarchs of israel

questions.enonce_markdown: The Israelites made a golden calf because:
questions.corrige_markdown: In Exodus 32 Moses stayed a long time on Mount Sinai, the people grew impatient and asked Aaron to make a god to go before them, so Aaron made the golden calf. Moses did not abandon the people or hand over to Aaron, who had simply been left in charge for the time being. **Answer: C.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - exodus and moses

choix.texte: Moses did not prepare them for the mission.

questions.enonce_markdown: The event that marked the Hebrews' departure from Egypt is known as:
questions.corrige_markdown: The word Exodus means 'going out', and it is the name given to the departure of the Hebrews from Egypt under Moses, which is also the name of the biblical book that tells it. The Passover (Exodus 12) commemorates the night when the Hebrew houses were spared and it immediately precedes the departure, so it is the closest distractor, while the covenant belongs to Sinai and the Exile is the later deportation to Babylon. **Answer: D.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - exodus and moses

questions.enonce_markdown: Samuel was called, while serving under the priest Eli at:
questions.corrige_markdown: In 1 Samuel 3 the boy Samuel was serving Eli in the sanctuary at Shiloh when God called him by name. Ramah was Samuel's home town and later his base as judge, Hebron is linked with Abraham and with David's early reign, and Jerusalem became the capital only under David. **Answer: C.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - judges and the monarchy

questions.enonce_markdown: The Israelites dissolved theocracy and replaced it with:
questions.corrige_markdown: Under the judges Israel was ruled as a theocracy, with God as the true king. When the elders asked Samuel for a king like the other nations (1 Samuel 8), the people replaced this system with a monarchy, first under Saul. **Answer: B.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - judges and the monarchy

questions.enonce_markdown:
King Saul came from the tribe of:

*Options as printed:* A) Kish.   B) Reuben.   C) Ephraim.   D) Gad.
questions.corrige_markdown:
Saul belonged to the tribe of Benjamin (1 Samuel 9): Kish was his father, a man of Benjamin, so Kish is a person and not a tribe. Reuben, Ephraim and Gad are other tribes of Israel, but none of them is Saul's tribe. The correct tribe, Benjamin, is not among the printed options, so no letter can be marked correct.



The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.
themes: A Level Religious Studies - judges and the monarchy

questions.enonce_markdown: He laid the foundation of the Temple in Jerusalem:
questions.corrige_markdown: Solomon began to build the Temple in Jerusalem in the fourth year of his reign (1 Kings 5 and 6). David had planned it and gathered materials but was not the one who built it, Absalom was David's rebellious son, and Samuel was the prophet who anointed Saul and David. **Answer: A.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - judges and the monarchy

questions.enonce_markdown: What did king Solomon request from God?
questions.corrige_markdown: In 1 Kings 3 God appeared to Solomon at Gibeon and invited him to ask for something. Solomon asked for an understanding mind to govern the people and to discern between good and evil, that is, wisdom, and God was pleased that he had not asked for wealth, long life or the death of his enemies. **Answer: C.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - judges and the monarchy

questions.enonce_markdown: In Jeremiah's letter to the Exiles, God promised to:
questions.corrige_markdown: In Jeremiah 29 the prophet writes to the exiles in Babylon, urging them to settle there, build houses and seek the welfare of the city, and he relays God's promise that after the period of exile God would bring them back to their land. The letter does not promise punishment of their oppressors and does not say that they will stay in exile for ever. **Answer: B.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - prophets of israel and judah

choix.texte: Bring them back to their land.

questions.enonce_markdown: Daniel was thrown into the lion's den during the reign of:
questions.corrige_markdown: Daniel 6 places the episode of the lions' den under Darius the Mede, after officials plotted against Daniel because of his prayer to God. Belshazzar is the king of the feast in Daniel 5, Nebuchadnezzar is the king of the fiery furnace and of the dreams (Daniel 2 to 4), and Jehoiachim (Jehoiakim or Jehoiachin) was a king of Judah, not a ruler in Daniel's court. **Answer: C.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - prophets of israel and judah

questions.enonce_markdown: In the book of Hosea, God desires genuine:
questions.corrige_markdown: Hosea 6:6 states that God desires steadfast love and not sacrifice, the knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings. The book as a whole presents God's faithful covenant love toward an unfaithful people, so love (loyalty) rather than ritual is what God is said to want. **Answer: B.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - prophets of israel and judah

questions.enonce_markdown: The main theme in prophet Amos' message is:
questions.corrige_markdown: Amos, a prophet of the eighth century BCE, condemned oppression of the poor, corrupt courts and empty worship, and called for justice to roll down like waters (Amos 5:24). Marriage is the image of Hosea's message, while sacrifice and worship are criticised by Amos when they are separated from justice. **Answer: D.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - prophets of israel and judah

questions.enonce_markdown: The Jewish desire to return to the land of Israel is known as:
questions.corrige_markdown: Zionism is the movement, organised in the late nineteenth century and associated with Theodor Herzl, that aims at a Jewish homeland in the land of Israel, which also expresses the older religious longing for Zion. Immigration and emigration only describe moving into or out of a country, and the Holocaust is the Nazi genocide of European Jews. **Answer: D.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - judaism

questions.enonce_markdown: All of these are branches of Judaism except:
questions.corrige_markdown: Reform, Orthodox and Conservative Judaism are three recognised branches of modern Judaism. 'Neo Judaism' is not the name of a recognised branch, so it is the exception. **Answer: C.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - judaism

questions.enonce_markdown: What is the Jewish day of Atonement?
questions.corrige_markdown: Yom Kippur is the Day of Atonement, the holiest day of the Jewish year, observed with fasting, prayer and repentance (Leviticus 16 and 23). Hanukkah (printed 'Hadikkah' in A and 'Hanukkah' in D) is the festival of lights that recalls the rededication of the Temple, and Passover recalls the Exodus from Egypt. **Answer: B.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - judaism

questions.enonce_markdown: What does it mean when it is said that Jewish food must be 'kosher'?
questions.corrige_markdown: 'Kosher' means fit or proper according to the Jewish dietary laws (kashrut), which are based on the Torah. Of the four options, 'clean' is the one that expresses this idea: kosher food is food that is permitted and prepared as the law requires, and it has nothing to do with being fresh, warm or boiled. **Answer: B.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - judaism

questions.enonce_markdown: The founder of Buddhism is:
questions.corrige_markdown: Buddhism was founded by Siddhartha Gautama (printed 'Siddharta'), a prince of the Shakya clan in northern India who, according to Buddhist tradition, became the Buddha, the 'awakened one', after his enlightenment. Ashoka was a later emperor who supported Buddhism, and 'Prince of Zen' and 'Sunja Boya' are not founders of Buddhism. **Answer: D.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - buddhism

questions.enonce_markdown: The path to end suffering in Buddhism is:
questions.corrige_markdown: The Buddha taught that the way leading to the end of suffering is the Noble Eightfold Path, which is the fourth of the Four Noble Truths. The Four Noble Truths set out the problem and its remedy (suffering, its cause, its end and the path) but the path itself is the eightfold path, while right conduct is only one of its parts and the five precepts are basic moral rules for lay people. **Answer: D.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - buddhism

questions.enonce_markdown: In Buddhism, the circle of rebirth is called:
questions.corrige_markdown: Samsara (printed 'Samrara') is the cycle of birth, death and rebirth that Buddhists seek to escape. Nirvana is the release from that cycle, Dharma is the teaching (and the natural law), and Tantra names a body of texts and practices. **Answer: D.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - buddhism

questions.enonce_markdown:
What does the lotus flower in Buddhism represent?

*Options as printed:* A) Wisdom.   B) Beauty.   C) Holiness.   D) Truth.
questions.corrige_markdown:
In Buddhist art the lotus is commonly said to stand for purity and spiritual awakening, because it grows out of muddy water and opens unstained. None of the four options states 'purity' or 'enlightenment' exactly, and wisdom, holiness and truth can each be linked to the symbol by different manuals, so no single letter can be marked correct.



The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.
themes: A Level Religious Studies - buddhism

questions.enonce_markdown: The law of the karma in Hinduism is:
questions.corrige_markdown: Karma is the law of cause and effect: every action, good or bad, has consequences that shape the future of the person, including future lives. The Four Noble Truths and the Eightfold Path are Buddhist teachings, and persuasion has nothing to do with karma. **Answer: A.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - hinduism

questions.enonce_markdown:
Hindu dogmas are found in:

*Options as printed:* A) Vedas.   B) Ashanyankas.   C) Brahmanas.   D) Upanishads.
questions.corrige_markdown:
The Vedas are the oldest and most authoritative scriptures of Hinduism, and the beliefs of the tradition are traced to them. The Brahmanas and the Upanishads are also parts of the wider Vedic literature, and 'Ashanyankas' does not match a scripture that can be identified, so several printed options could be defended.

**Intended answer: A (Vedas).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.
themes: A Level Religious Studies - hinduism

questions.enonce_markdown: What is the ultimate reality in Hinduism?
questions.corrige_markdown: In Hindu philosophy Brahman is the ultimate, unchanging reality, the source and ground of everything that exists. The Vedas and the Puranas are scriptures, and moksha is liberation, not the ultimate reality itself. **Answer: B.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - hinduism

questions.enonce_markdown: The liberation of the soul from the wheel of life in Hinduism is called:
questions.corrige_markdown: Moksha (printed 'Mosksha') is liberation from samsara, the wheel of birth, death and rebirth. A Purana is a scripture, Brahman is the ultimate reality, and Amman is not the term for this liberation. **Answer: B.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - hinduism

questions.enonce_markdown:
The Hindu religion is spread through:

*Options as printed:* A) Dharma.   B) Kharma.   C) Yoga.   D) Nirvana.
questions.corrige_markdown:
Hinduism has no single founder and is not mainly spread by missionary preaching. Among the printed options, dharma (sacred duty and the order of life, the very name by which Hindus often describe their tradition) is the most plausible, but the wording 'is spread through' is vague, and karma (printed 'Kharma') and yoga could also be linked to it.

**Intended answer: A (Dharma).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.
themes: A Level Religious Studies - hinduism

questions.enonce_markdown: Who is the first prophet in Islam?
questions.corrige_markdown: Islamic tradition holds that Adam was the first human being and the first prophet. Ibrahim (Abraham), Issa (Jesus) and Daouda (David) came after him in the line of prophets recognised in Islam. **Answer: A.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - prophets in islam

questions.enonce_markdown: The word 'Islam' is a noun which is formed from the Arabic verb meaning?
questions.corrige_markdown: 'Islam' comes from the Arabic root s-l-m and means submission to the will of God, with a link to peace. A Muslim is one who submits, so the verb meaning is 'to submit'. **Answer: D.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - islamic worship and practices

questions.enonce_markdown: Who was the first convert of Prophet Muhammad into Islam?
questions.corrige_markdown: According to Muslim tradition, Khadija, the Prophet's wife, was the first person to believe in his message after the first revelation. Ali (a young cousin) and Abu Bakr (printed 'Abu Bar', a close friend) are also named among the earliest believers, as the first youth and the first adult man, while Umar accepted Islam later. **Answer: C.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - life of prophet muhammad

questions.enonce_markdown: Who is the last prophet in Islam?
questions.corrige_markdown: Muslims believe that Muhammad is the last of the prophets, called the Seal of the Prophets (Qur'an 33:40). Musa (Moses) and Daouda (David) are earlier prophets, and Ali was the Prophet's cousin and the fourth caliph, not a prophet. **Answer: D.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - prophets in islam

questions.enonce_markdown: Which is the month of fasting in Islam?
questions.corrige_markdown: Ramadan, the ninth month of the Islamic calendar, is the month in which Muslims fast from dawn to sunset, and fasting (sawm) is one of the five pillars. Muharram, Rajab and Shaban are other months of the Islamic calendar. **Answer: B.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - five pillars of islam

questions.enonce_markdown: The part of his income which the Muslim is required to give as zakat is:
questions.corrige_markdown: Zakat, the third pillar of Islam, is the obligatory yearly almsgiving of 2.5 per cent on the wealth and savings that a Muslim holds above a minimum threshold (the nisab) for a year. Of the printed options, 2.5% is the correct rate, and 10% resembles the tithe of other traditions. **Answer: B.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - five pillars of islam

questions.enonce_markdown: The Angel who visited Prophet Muhammad with a call for his mission was:
questions.corrige_markdown: Muslim tradition holds that the angel Jibril (Gabriel) came to Muhammad in the cave of Hira and brought the first revelation that called him to his mission. Mikail (Michael) and Izrafil are other angels in Islamic tradition and are not the angel of revelation. **Answer: C.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - life of prophet muhammad

questions.enonce_markdown: The number of Surahs in the Qur'an is:
questions.corrige_markdown: The Qur'an is divided into 114 surahs (chapters) of varying length. The other numbers do not match the Qur'an. **Answer: C.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - islamic scriptures and law

questions.enonce_markdown: The longest Surah in the Qur'an is:
questions.corrige_markdown: The longest surah is Al-Baqarah (The Cow), the second surah in the order of the Qur'an, with 286 verses. The first surah, Al-Fatiha, is very short. **Answer: B.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - islamic scriptures and law

questions.enonce_markdown: The shrine in Arabia that is focused on an annual pilgrimage is:
questions.corrige_markdown: The Ka'ba in Mecca is the sacred shrine toward which Muslims pray and around which the pilgrims walk during the annual pilgrimage. Hajj is the name of the pilgrimage itself, not the shrine, 'Kabala' is not a shrine of Islam, and 'Sawn' (sawm) is fasting. **Answer: A.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - five pillars of islam

questions.enonce_markdown: After the death of Muhammad, who succeeded him?
questions.corrige_markdown: After the death of the Prophet in 632 CE the leadership of the Muslim community passed to the caliphs (khalifa means successor), the first of whom was Abu Bakr. Umar al Khattab was the second caliph, not the one who first succeeded him, and 'Al-Hajj' is a title for one who has made the pilgrimage. 'Imams' is the title used for the leaders of the community in Shi'a belief, so the printed question is read here in its common historical sense of the caliphs. **Answer: B.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - islamic community and leadership

questions.enonce_markdown: Muslims go on annual pilgrimage to:
questions.corrige_markdown: The Hajj, the fifth pillar of Islam, is performed every year in Mecca, around the Ka'ba. Mina is a place near Mecca where some rites are performed, Medina holds the Prophet's mosque and is visited but is not the place of the Hajj, and Jerusalem is a holy city but not the place of the pilgrimage. **Answer: C.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - five pillars of islam

questions.enonce_markdown: The largest Muslim grouping in the world is:
questions.corrige_markdown: The Sunnis form the large majority of Muslims worldwide. The Shi'a are the second largest group, and the Wahhabi movement and the Tijani brotherhood (printed 'Wahabis' and 'Tijannis') are smaller movements within Sunni Islam. **Answer: A.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - islamic community and leadership

questions.enonce_markdown: Where do the dead go to in ATR?
questions.corrige_markdown: In African Traditional Religion, as the classical authors present it, death is not the end of life: the dead are believed to pass into the spirit world, the world of the ancestors, which can be described in general terms as the hereafter. Paradise, hell and purgatory are ideas belonging to other religious traditions. These are generalities that vary from one people to another. **Answer: D.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - atr beliefs and practices

questions.enonce_markdown:
It is considered in ATR as a curse:

*Options as printed:* A) Suicide.   B) Poverty.   C) Polyandry.   D) Superstition.
questions.corrige_markdown:
In many African traditional societies a curse is understood as a spoken or ritual invocation of harm that is believed to take effect when someone has broken the moral or social order, for example by violating a taboo or wronging a person. The question does not name a single classic fact of the programme, and which of the four printed conditions is regarded as a curse depends on the community, so no single letter can be marked correct.



The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.
themes: A Level Religious Studies - atr beliefs and practices

questions.enonce_markdown: Ancestors in ATR are known as:
questions.corrige_markdown: In the writing of John Mbiti and other authors on ATR, the ancestors are called the 'living-dead': they have died physically but remain remembered by their families, stay part of the community and are believed to watch over it. They are not simply dead, not gods and not divine. **Answer: C.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - atr beliefs and practices

questions.enonce_markdown:
The major type of worship in ATR is:

*Options as printed:* A) Veneration of ancestors.   B) Animism.   C) Sorcery.   D) Human sacrifice.
questions.corrige_markdown:
Many textbooks describe the veneration of ancestors, with libations, offerings and prayers, as a central practice of ATR, alongside the worship of the Supreme Being and respect for divinities. Sorcery and human sacrifice are not presented as forms of worship, and 'animism' is a label that many scholars of ATR consider unsuitable. Which practice is the 'major' one depends on the author, so these are generalities.

**Intended answer: A (Veneration of ancestors).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.
themes: A Level Religious Studies - atr beliefs and practices

questions.enonce_markdown:
What is the essence of African morality?

*Options as printed:* A) Good conduct.   B) Wellbeing.   C) Customs.   D) Community life.
questions.corrige_markdown:
Authors on ATR stress that African morality is community-centred: conduct is judged by its effect on relationships and on the life of the group, which is summed up in the saying 'I am because we are'. Good conduct and customs are also mentioned in manuals, and the emphasis differs between authors, which is why a single letter cannot be marked with certainty.

**Intended answer: D (Community life).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.
themes: A Level Religious Studies - atr beliefs and practices

questions.enonce_markdown: ATR is highly dependable on the following except :
questions.corrige_markdown: ATR has no founder and no central sacred book, so it is handed down by word of mouth through myths, proverbs, songs, rituals and festivals, and it gives a central place to ancestors. Its dependence on written tradition is therefore the exception. **Answer: C.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - atr beliefs and practices

questions.enonce_markdown: In ATR, they are believed to be next to God:
questions.corrige_markdown: In the classical presentation of ATR the Supreme Being is served by divinities, lesser spiritual beings that act as his agents and are placed next to him in the order of spiritual beings. The dead (ancestors), medicine men and diviners are closer to human life, and the diviners and medicine men are human intermediaries. These are generalities that vary between peoples. **Answer: B.**
themes: A Level Religious Studies - atr beliefs and practices
